The HTTP/3 Protocol
The HTTP/3 Protocol element represents a Protocol Handler component that supports the HTTP/3 protocol (RFC 9114) over the QUIC transport (RFC 9000).
Unlike HTTP/2, HTTP/3 is not an upgrade of an existing protocol: it runs directly over UDP and always uses TLS 1.3 (RFC 9001). An HTTP/3 connector is therefore configured as a standalone connector by setting its protocol attribute to one of the HTTP/3 protocol classes and its SSLEnabled attribute to true. The protocol class also selects the QUIC transport implementation: org.apache.coyote.http3.Http3OpenSSLProtocol uses the OpenSSL QUIC endpoint, org.apache.coyote.http3.Http3QuicheProtocol uses the Cloudflare quiche endpoint. Certificates are configured through nested SSLHostConfig and Certificate elements, as described in the HTTP Connector document. The OpenSSL QUIC endpoint accepts PEM files (with the key and certificate chain supplied separately), PKCS#12 files and Java keystores; the quiche endpoint currently loads its certificate from PEM files.
HTTP/3 support requires the FFM bindings to be compiled into the build (a current JDK) plus a usable QUIC transport: for Http3OpenSSLProtocol, an OpenSSL installation that provides the QUIC API (OpenSSL 4.0 or later) loaded into the JVM via the FFM bindings - see the OpenSSLLifecycleListener configuration in the default conf/server.xml; for Http3QuicheProtocol, a loadable libquiche. The connector fails at bind time when the selected transport is unusable. The sample conf/server.xml also configures a TLS connector on the TCP side of the same port with altService="h3" so that HTTP/3 is discovered by clients through the Alt-Svc response header.
The HTTP/3 protocol handler supports the following attributes on the connector:
The alternative service which should be advertised as available to clients via the Alt-Svc response header. The value is a protocol identifier, for example h3; the port advertised is the port of the request the header is added to. An Alt-Svc header set by the application takes precedence. If not specified, no Alt-Svc header is added.
A boolean value which can be used to enable or disable the consistency check for the scheme presented by the user agent in the :scheme pseudo-header and the channel over which the request was received. Since QUIC always uses TLS, the consistent scheme is https. This should only be set to true where a trusted TLS terminating reverse proxy is used. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
The value is a comma separated list of MIME types for which HTTP compression may be used. The default value is
text/html,text/xml,text/plain,text/css,text/javascript,application/javascript,application/json,application/xml . If you specify a type explicitly, the default is over-ridden.
The Connector may use GZIP compression in an attempt to save server bandwidth. The acceptable values for the parameter is "off" (disable compression), "on" (allow compression, which causes text data to be compressed), "force" (forces compression in all cases), or a numerical integer value (which is equivalent to "on", but specifies the minimum amount of data before the output is compressed). If the content-length is not known and compression is set to "on" or more aggressive, the output will also be compressed. If not specified, this attribute is set to "off".
Note that HTTP/3 forbids the Transfer-Encoding header (RFC 9114 Section 4.2). A request whose TE header carries any value other than trailers — including one that asks for compression through TE rather than through Accept-Encoding — is rejected as a malformed field section.
If compression is set to "on" then this attribute may be used to specify the minimum amount of data before the output is compressed. If not specified, this attribute is defaults to "2048". Units are in bytes.
When to respond with a 100 intermediate response code to a request containing an Expect: 100-continue header. The following values may be used:
immediately (the default) - an intermediate 100 status response will be returned as soon as practical
onRead - an intermediate 100 status response will be returned only when the Servlet reads the request body, allowing the servlet to inspect the headers and possibly respond before the user agent sends a possibly large request body.
A boolean value which controls whether Extended CONNECT (RFC 9220) is permitted. When enabled, the value 1 is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL and requests carrying a :protocol pseudo-header are accepted. Note that the tunnel established by Extended CONNECT cannot yet carry application data because HTTP datagrams (RFC 9297) are not yet implemented. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
A boolean value which controls whether Tomcat advertises the experimental, unregistered H2_COMPATIBLE_IDENTITY setting (identifier 0x22). Peers that do not recognise the setting ignore it. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
The QUIC connection idle timeout in milliseconds (RFC 9000 Section 10.1). If no packet is received from the peer for this duration the connection is closed. The value is also advertised to the peer in the TLS transport parameters so that both endpoints agree on the timeout. If not specified, a default of 30000 (30 seconds) is used.
The maximum number of active request streams permitted for any one connection. If a client attempts to open more active streams than this limit, the additional streams are refused. The effective limit is clamped to the limit the QUIC transport actually advertises to the peer. If not specified, a default of 100 is used.
The maximum field section size, in bytes, that this endpoint is willing to decode (RFC 9114 Section 4.2.2). The value is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE and enforced on incoming field sections. If not specified, a default of 16384 is used.
A comma-separated list of content encodings that indicate already-compressed content. When the response already has a Content-Encoding header with one of these values, compression will not be applied to prevent double compression. This attribute is only used if compression is set to on or force.
If not specified, the default value is br,compress,dcb,dcz,deflate,gzip,pack200-gzip,zstd, which includes all commonly used compression algorithms.
The value is a regular expression (using java.util.regex) matching the entire user-agent header of HTTP clients for which compression should not be used, because these clients, although they do advertise support for the feature, have a broken implementation. The default value is an empty String (regexp matching disabled).
The maximum number of request streams per connection that may block waiting for dynamic table entries announced on the peer's QPACK encoder stream (RFC 9204 Section 2.1.2). A positive value is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS. A value of 0 disables stream blocking: field sections that reference entries not yet present in the dynamic table are then treated as a decompression failure. If not specified, a default of 0 is used.
The maximum QPACK dynamic table capacity in bytes. The value is advertised to peers via SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY and the local decoder is sized to match, as required for interoperability (RFC 9204 Section 5). A value of 0 disables the dynamic table entirely. If not specified, a default of 4096 is used.
The value used for the Server header in any HTTP/3 response created by this connector. If configured, it always overrides any value the application may have set. If not specified, no Server header is set by the connector; an application-provided value stands unless serverRemoveAppProvidedValues is enabled.
If set to true, any Server header provided by the application is removed from HTTP/3 responses when no server value is configured. If not specified, this attribute is set to false.
The following connector attributes are handled by the QUIC endpoint that backs the HTTP/3 protocol handler:
The maximum number of concurrent QUIC connections the endpoint accepts. Connections opened above this limit are refused. If not specified, a default of 8192 is used.
The timeout, in milliseconds, used for each iteration of the endpoint's QUIC poll loop. Smaller values reduce event latency at the cost of more frequent wake-ups. Values outside the range 1 to 60000 are rejected with a warning and the previous value is retained. If not specified, a default of 10 is used.
The size, in bytes, of the per-stream read buffer maintained by the endpoint. Values below 1 are rejected with a warning and the previous value is retained. Stream data is drained in chunks of at most 65536 bytes by the quiche endpoint, whose native read buffer is capped at the maximum datagram size; the OpenSSL endpoint reads up to the buffer's remaining capacity in a single call. Either way, larger values are filled by repeated reads. If not specified, a default of 16384 is used.
Upper bound, in milliseconds, of the adaptive floor the OpenSSL QUIC endpoint's poll loop applies to due-deadline (timer) ticks: while such ticks fire back-to-back without any reactive work, the floor doubles from 20 ms up to this value, coalescing the ticks; it resets as soon as the loop performs reactive work. A value of 0 disables the floor, running every tick the engine reports as due. Values outside the range 0 to 60000 are rejected with a warning and the previous value is retained. If not specified, a default of 50 is used. The quiche endpoint has no due-tick floor and does not support this attribute.
The HTTP/3 connector also supports the following attributes, which are documented in the HTTP Connector document:
allowedTrailerHeaders
maxHeaderCount
maxThreads
relaxedPathChars
relaxedQueryChars
Note that send file support is not available over QUIC: response bodies are always written through the output buffer as HTTP/3 DATA frames.
An HTTP/3 connector requires at least one nested SSLHostConfig element since QUIC mandates TLS 1.3. Each SSLHostConfig needs at least one Certificate or PreSharedKey element. These elements are the same as those used by the HTTP Connector.
TLS 1.3 external pre-shared keys are supported by the OpenSSL QUIC endpoint; the quiche endpoint does not support them. A connection that offers a configured identity is authenticated with the pre-shared key and the server presents no certificate. An SSLHostConfig that has both certificates and pre-shared keys serves both: connections with a resolvable identity get a pre-shared key handshake, connections with an unknown identity or with no identity at all get the normal certificate handshake. An SSLHostConfig configured with pre-shared keys only presents no certificate; a connection that does not offer a usable identity then fails the handshake.
Client certificates (mutual TLS) are not supported: the certificateVerification attribute of SSLHostConfig is ignored by both QUIC endpoints and no client certificate is ever requested during the TLS handshake. The quiche endpoint logs a warning at start-up when the attribute is configured with a value other than none.
TLS session resumption is supported by both QUIC endpoints through TLS 1.3 session tickets: the server issues a ticket after each handshake and a client offering a ticket from an earlier connection to the same endpoint completes the handshake without a full key exchange. The ticket keys are generated randomly when the endpoint starts, so a ticket is only valid for the running endpoint instance that issued it: after a restart (and, for the quiche endpoint, after a certificate reload, which rebuilds the TLS configuration) older tickets can no longer be decrypted and a client offering one simply performs a full handshake. Ticket keys are not configurable, so tickets do not span separate Tomcat instances. The OpenSSL QUIC endpoint honours the disableSessionTickets attribute of SSLHostConfig; the quiche endpoint has no equivalent switch and always issues tickets.
HTTP/3 connections are discovered by clients through the Alt-Svc response header. The usual arrangement is a TLS connector on the TCP side of the same port with altService="h3" announcing the HTTP/3 endpoint, as shown in the default conf/server.xml. An HTTP/3 connector does not announce itself automatically; set its altService attribute when an announcement from the HTTP/3 side is wanted.
Response compression is not implemented for HTTP/3. The HTTP/1.1 connector's compression configuration does not apply to HTTP/3 responses; any content coding must be applied by the application.
